lede: Cut a slice out of a pizza and you have a sector: two straight edges and a curved crust. The angle at the centre says what fraction of the whole circle the slice is, and that one fraction gives both the length of its crust and the amount of pizza on it. One idea, used twice.
can: Turn the angle at the centre into a fraction of a full turn.
Work out an arc length as that fraction of the circumference.
Work out a sector area as that fraction of the circle's area.

md: A sector is a fraction of a circle, and the angle at the centre names the fraction: turn through $90°$ out of $360°$ and you have taken a quarter of the rim and a quarter of the inside. The other pieces have names of their own — a tangent, a chord, an arc, a segment. Nothing in this topic is printed on the Higher formula sheet, so all four circle formulae are memory.

prompt: A full turn is 360°. What fraction of a whole circle is a 90° sector? Give your answer as a fraction or a decimal.
explain: Yes: 90 out of 360 is a quarter. Every arc and sector question starts with this one idea.

md:
A sector is a **fraction of a circle**, and the angle at the centre is what names the fraction. Turn through $\theta$ degrees out of the full $360°$ and you have taken $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of everything the circle has: that fraction of the rim, and that fraction of the inside.

So there is really only one formula, used twice:

**Arc length** $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$ — a fraction of the **circumference**.
**Sector area** $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$ — the same fraction of the **area**.

Write the fraction first, work out the whole circle second, multiply third. That order keeps the two apart.

prompt: Which one is the arc length of a sector of radius $r$ and angle $\theta$?
explain: Yes. An arc is part of the rim, so it grows out of the circumference 2πr. The other line is the sector area, and it would come out in square units.

title: Why one fraction does both jobs
md: Think of the circle as $360$ identical one-degree slivers. Each sliver carries $\dfrac{1}{360}$ of the rim and $\dfrac{1}{360}$ of the inside, so $\theta$ of them carry $\dfrac{\theta}{360}$ of each. That is why the same fraction multiplies the circumference for an arc and the area for a sector.

title: Nothing here is on the formula sheet
md:
$C = 2\pi r$, $A = \pi r^2$, arc $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$, sector $= \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$. Four formulae, all from memory.
A quick check on any answer: the arc must be **shorter than the whole circumference**, and the sector area **smaller than the whole circle**.

prompt: A sector has radius 5 cm and angle 72°. Its arc is $\dfrac{72}{360} \times 2\pi(5)$. What is that, to 1 decimal place?
explain: 72/360 is one fifth, and one fifth of 31.4159 cm is 6.2832 cm, so 6.3 cm to 1 decimal place.

title: Arc Length
why: Four minutes on the fraction idea, worked slowly. Watch how the fraction is written down before any button is pressed — that is the line the mark scheme wants to see.

prompt: In the video, what is written down before the calculator is used?
answer: The fraction of the circle, θ/360
explain: Yes. Writing the fraction first is what earns the method mark, even if the arithmetic afterwards goes wrong.
options: The fraction of the circle, θ/360

text: Perimeter means the whole way round

md:
A perimeter is the distance round the **outside**, and a sector's outside is partly curved and partly straight. Trace it: out along one radius, round the arc, back along the other radius.

**Perimeter of a sector** $=$ arc $+\ 2r$.

A semicircle works the same way: the curved part is half the circumference, and the straight part is the diameter, so the perimeter is $\pi r + 2r$.

prompt: A sector has radius 6 cm and an arc of 10 cm. What is its perimeter, in cm?
explain: Yes: 10 + 6 + 6 = 22 cm. Two radii, because you travel along a straight edge twice.

title: November 2024, M3 Q20 and M4 Q5
md:
Both papers asked for the **perimeter of a semicircle**. Most candidates halved the circumference and stopped. Two marks out of three was the typical score.
The fix is not more formulae: it is putting your finger on the diagram and following the edge all the way round before you write the total.

text: Major or minor: read the diagram

md:
Two points on a circle give **two** arcs: the short way round (the **minor** arc) and the long way round (the **major** arc). The angle printed at the centre is usually the minor one, so if the diagram draws the long way round you need $360 - \theta$ first.

A free check: the two arcs must add up to the circumference.

prompt: The angle at the centre is 100° and the major arc is wanted. Which angle do you use, in degrees?
explain: Yes: 360 − 100 = 260. The major arc is everything the marked angle leaves behind.

md:
On a non-calculator paper you are asked to leave the answer **in terms of $\pi$**. Treat $\pi$ as a symbol you carry through, cancel the fraction first, and never replace it with 3.14.

For a sector of radius 15 cm and angle 24°: the circumference is $30\pi$, the fraction $\dfrac{24}{360}$ is $\dfrac{1}{15}$, and $\dfrac{30\pi}{15} = 2\pi$ cm.

A perimeter then stays as two pieces, for example $(4\pi + 18)$ cm: a multiple of $\pi$ and a whole number cannot be added.

prompt: A sector of radius 12 cm has an angle of 30°. Write its arc length in terms of $\pi$.
explain: 30/360 is one twelfth, and one twelfth of 24π is 2π cm.

task: Drag the angle from small to reflex and watch the arc and the area change together. Stop at a reflex angle and predict, before you read it, whether the arc is more or less than half the circumference.

prompt: In the applet, what happens to the sector area when you double the angle from 40° to 80°?
explain: Yes: the fraction θ/360 doubles and the circle's area does not change, so the sector area doubles. Doubling the radius would be different — that multiplies the area by four.

md:
Turn the angle at the centre into a fraction of a full turn.
Take that fraction of the circumference for an arc, of the area for a sector.
Add the two radii when a perimeter is asked for.
Use $360 - \theta$ when the major arc is the one drawn.

Expect one three-mark question in the second half of the paper. The first mark is the fraction of the turn together with the right whole-circle formula; the last is the answer rounded exactly as asked, in cm for an arc or a perimeter and cm² for an area. Stuck: work out the circumference or the area of the whole circle anyway — it scores, and it shows which formula the question wanted.
